name: APT38
aliases: Lazarus Group (parent umbrella, see separate profile)
description: APT38 (BlueNoroff) is the financial-crime-focused cluster of North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau cyber apparatus, historically responsible for SWIFT-network bank heists (Bangladesh Bank, $81M, 2016) and the FASTCash ATM cash-out scheme that hit banks across dozens of countries. The group has since pivoted almost entirely to cryptocurrency exchanges and DeFi platforms, executing the largest crypto theft in history — the ~$1.5B Bybit/Safe{Wallet} heist in February 2025 — via a compromised macOS developer workstation and stolen AWS session tokens. In 2026, BlueNoroff continues high-tempo operations against crypto and fintech firms using typosquatted Zoom/Calendly meeting lures and ClickFix clipboard-injection malware, including a confirmed intrusion at a North American crypto company in January 2026 and the March 2026 Bitrefill breach. APT38's tradecraft remains distinguished by patient, multi-month operations culminating in precisely-timed, custom-tailored cash-out and laundering operations.

ttps.notes: Stolen AWS/cloud session tokens from compromised developer workstations used to bypass MFA (Bybit/Safe{Wallet} heist)

ttps.technique_name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
ttps.notes: Compromise of trusted third-party wallet/vendor software (Safe{Wallet}) to inject malicious transaction-signing logic
PyYAML RCE exploited via trojanized crypto-themed Python application delivered to a macOS developer
Typosquatted Zoom meeting links delivered through manipulated Calendly invites to crypto-firm employees
ClickFix-style clipboard injection tricks victims into pasting and executing malicious PowerShell commands
Injection of malicious JavaScript into web app frontends to silently redirect cryptocurrency transactions to attacker wallets
FASTCash: manipulation of payment switch application responses to approve fraudulent ATM withdrawals
Core mission objective — SWIFT transfer fraud, ATM cash-outs, and exchange/bridge fund redirection

notable_techniques: Bybit/Safe{Wallet} heist (Feb 2025, ~$1.5B in ETH) — single compromised macOS developer credential escalated into full transaction-signing compromise of a major exchange's cold wallet workflow
FASTCash — modifies responses from compromised payment switch application servers to authorize fraudulent ATM cash-outs simultaneously across many countries within minutes
Long-dwell, surveillance-heavy operations — months of reconnaissance on victim banking/exchange infrastructure before executing a heist on a precisely timed weekend or holiday window
Typosquatted Zoom/Calendly lures combined with ClickFix clipboard hijacking to gain initial access at crypto and fintech firms
Funds laundered at speed through chain-hopping, mixers, and OTC brokers immediately following theft to outpace freezing/recovery efforts
Use of legitimate cloud session tokens (not just credentials) to fully bypass MFA on cloud-hosted wallet infrastructure
detection_opportunities: Anomalous SWIFT/payment-switch message volume or off-hours fund transfers, especially around weekends/holidays
ATM cash-out spikes occurring near-simultaneously across geographically dispersed locations
Calendly/meeting-invite links resolving to typosquatted Zoom domains (e.g. zoom-us, zoorn, etc.)
Clipboard-paste-and-run prompts (ClickFix) presented to users via fake verification or meeting-fix dialogs
Cloud session token reuse from new geolocations or devices shortly after a developer workstation compromise
Unexpected modifications to transaction-signing or wallet frontend JavaScript at exchanges/custodians
Outbound traffic from finance/crypto custody systems to newly registered or recently re-activated C2 infrastructure
response_playbook: Review SWIFT/payment-switch logs for anomalous message volume or off-hours fund transfers, especially around weekends/holidays.
Audit calendar/meeting invites for typosquatted Zoom/Calendly domains and ClickFix-style 'paste to fix' prompts.
Inspect cloud session tokens for reuse from new geolocations or devices, particularly around wallet/exchange infrastructure.
Check transaction-signing or wallet front-end JavaScript for unauthorized modifications.
Trace any developer-workstation compromise forward to downstream cold-wallet or transaction-signing access.
If financial theft is confirmed, immediately engage exchange/banking partners and blockchain-analysis firms for chain-hopping and mixer tracing.
